text.title: Agency Valuation Rubric Core Rules
text.summary: 6 testable rules for building and applying the weighted rubric: what the multiplier is allowed to multiply, how criteria and their anchors must be constructed so two raters agree, how owner dependency is split, and why the score-to-multiplier map must be bounded by real comparables.

rule.statement: `ebitda_usd` MUST be normalized before any multiplier is applied, and the artefact records the bridge line by line: owner compensation restated to the market rate for the role actually performed, non-recurring and personal expenses removed, and the cost of replacing owner-delivered production added as an expense.
rule.rationale: The rubric is a multiplier, so error in the base propagates proportionally: scoring twelve criteria to one decimal on top of an un-normalized EBITDA produces a precise number attached to a wrong quantity, and the whole exercise is re-run once the buyer's accountant rebuilds the bridge.

rule.statement: No two weighted criteria may be driven by the same underlying quantity. Retainer share, recurring-revenue share and contracted backlog all proxy revenue predictability — at most one may carry weight, or their combined weight must be capped at the weight the single concept was intended to have.
rule.rationale: Correlated criteria behave as one criterion carrying the sum of their weights. An agency that is strong on predictability then scores high three times, the intended weighting silently changes, and the rubric stops discriminating between agencies that differ on everything else.

rule.statement: Every level 1 through 5 of every criterion MUST carry an observable anchor, not an adjective. Example anchor for owner-dependency level 5: "owner is primary contact on no account and bills under 5% of delivery hours". "Strong", "moderate", "good" are rejected.

rationale.source: Behaviorally Anchored Rating Scales — Smith & Kendall (1963)

rule.rationale: Adjectival scales give raters no shared referent, so the same agency scores 2 from one rater and 4 from another. Since the weighted total is compared across targets and across years, an unreproducible score makes every comparison the rubric exists to support invalid.

rule.statement: Owner dependency MUST be scored as two separate criteria: relationship dependency (share of revenue where the owner is the primary client contact) and delivery dependency (share of delivery hours billed by the owner). A single blended owner-dependency score is rejected.

rationale.source: Agency M&A — transferability of relationships vs transferability of capacity

rule.rationale: The two are priced differently. Delegated delivery but owner-held relationships is a transfer risk the buyer prices with an earnout tied to client retention; owner-held delivery is priced with a hiring cost inside EBITDA. A blended score hides which instrument the buyer will reach for.

rule.statement: The `weighted_total` to `multiplier` function MUST be monotonic, stated explicitly in the artefact, and bounded at both ends by an observed comparable-transaction range for the target's EBITDA band — sub-$1M EBITDA agencies and $2M+ EBITDA agencies do not share a band.
rule.rationale: An unbounded linear map lets a high rubric score generate a multiple no buyer in that size band has paid. The number then becomes the seller's anchor, offers arrive below it, and the founder rejects market-rate offers because an internal spreadsheet promised more.

rule.statement: The weight vector MUST be written down and frozen before the first target is scored, and reused unchanged across every target in the comparison set and across re-runs of the same target over time.

rationale.source: Pre-registration of decision criteria — MCDA practice

rule.rationale: Weights adjusted after the scores are visible convert the rubric into a justification for a decision already taken. Worse, a per-target weight vector means each target was measured with a different yardstick, so the ranking carries no information beyond the analyst's preference ordering.
